Machine learning models have shown great promise as decoders for the surface code; however, this promise has not yet been substantiated for the more challenging task of decoding quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes. In this paper, we present a recurrent, transformer-based neural network designed to decode circuit-level noise on Bivariate Bicycle (BB) codes. For the [MATH] BB code, at a physical error rate of [MATH], our model achieves logical error rates almost [MATH] times lower than belief propagation with ordered statistics decoding (BP-OSD), and roughly [MATH] times larger than a most-likely error decoder. Moreover, while BP-OSD has a wide distribution of runtimes with significant outliers, our model has a consistent runtime and is an order-of-magnitude faster than the worst-case times from a benchmark BP-OSD implementation. On the [MATH] BB code, our model obtains worse logical error rates but maintains the speed advantage. These results provide initial evidence that machine learning decoders can out-perform conventional decoders on small QLDPC codes, but suggest more complex architectures and/or training procedures are necessary to scale to larger code sizes.

.
tldr: This paper applies machine learning to decode circuit-level noise for bivariate bicycle codes, a type of quantum LDPC code.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires efficient decoders; machine learning decoders have shown promise for surface codes but not yet for QLDPC codes.
method: A recurrent, transformer-based neural network is designed to decode circuit-level noise on bivariate bicycle codes.
result: For the [[144,12,12]] BB code, the model achieves logical error rates almost 10 times lower than BP-OSD and is an order of magnitude faster, but for larger codes performance degrades.
conclusion: Machine learning decoders can outperform conventional decoders on small QLDPC codes, but scaling to larger codes requires more complex architectures.

title: On The Significance Of Wigner’s Friend In Contexts Beyond Quantum Foundations
authors: Caroline L. Jones And Markus P. Mueller
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2147 (2026).

There has been a surge of recent interest in the Wigner's Friend paradox, sparking several novel thought experiments and no-go theorems. The main narrative has been that Wigner's Friend highlights a counterintuitive feature that is unique to quantum theory, and which is closely related to the quantum measurement problem. Here, we challenge this view. We argue that the gist of the Wigner's Friend paradox can be reproduced without assuming quantum physics, and that it underlies a much broader class of enigmas in the foundations of physics and philosophy. To show this, we first consider several recently proposed Extended Wigner's Friend scenarios, and demonstrate that some of their implications for the absoluteness of observations can be reproduced by classical thought experiments that involve the duplication of agents. Crucially, some of these classical scenarios are technologically much easier to implement than their quantum counterparts. Then, we argue that the essential structural ingredient of all these scenarios is a feature that we call "Restriction A": that a physical theory cannot give us a probabilistic description of the observations of all agents. Finally, we argue that this difficulty is at the core of other puzzles in the foundations of physics and philosophy, and demonstrate this explicitly for cosmology's Boltzmann brain problem. Our analysis suggests that Wigner's Friend should be studied in a larger context, addressing a frontier of human knowledge beyond quantum foundations: to obtain reliable predictions for experiments in which these predictions can be privately but not intersubjectively verified.

.
tldr: The paper argues that the Wigner's Friend paradox is not unique to quantum theory but can be reproduced classically, and relates it to broader foundational puzzles.
motivation: To challenge the view that Wigner's Friend highlights a uniquely quantum feature and to show its relevance to other foundational problems.
method: The authors construct classical thought experiments that mimic extended Wigner's Friend scenarios and identify a common structural feature called 'Restriction A'.
result: They demonstrate that some implications of Wigner's Friend can be reproduced classically, and that the paradox shares structure with the Boltzmann brain problem.
conclusion: Wigner's Friend should be studied in a broader context beyond quantum foundations, addressing issues of private versus intersubjective verification.

title: Qubit Operations Using A Modular Optical System Engineered With PyOpticL: A code-to-CAD Optical Layout Tool
authors: Jacob Myers, Christopher Caron, Nishat Helaly, Zhenyu Wei, Justin Oh, Zack Gotobed, Kotaro Yabe, And Robert J. Niffenegger
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2135 (2026).

Complex optical design is hindered by conventional piecewise setup, which prevents modularization and therefore abstraction of subsystems at the circuit level. This limits multiple fields that require complex optics systems, including quantum computing with atoms and trapped ions, because their optical systems are not scalable. We present an open-source Python library for optical layout (PyOpticL) which uses beam-path simulation and dynamic beam-path routing for quick and easy optical layout by placing optical elements along the beam path without a priori specification, enabling adaptive, path-based layouts with automatic routing and connectivity. We use PyOpticL to create modular `drop-in' optical baseplates for common optical subsystems used in atomic and molecular optics (AMO) experiments including laser sources, frequency and intensity modulation, and locking to an atomic reference for stabilization. We demonstrate this minimal working example of a dynamic full laser system for strontium trapped ions by using it for laser cooling, qubit state detection, and over 99% fidelity single-qubit gates with 3D printed baseplates. This enables a new paradigm of design abstraction layers for engineering optical systems leveraging modular baseplates, as they can be used for any wavelength in the system and enables scaling up the underlying optical systems for quantum computers. This new open-source hardware and software code-to-CAD library seeks to foster open-source collaborative hardware and systems design across numerous fields of research including AMO physics and quantum computing with neutral atoms and trapped ions.

.
tldr: This paper presents PyOpticL, an open-source Python library for modular optical layout, and demonstrates its use for building a laser system for trapped-ion qubit operations.
motivation: Complex optical design in quantum computing with atoms and trapped ions is hindered by conventional piecewise setup, which prevents modularization and scalability.
method: The authors developed PyOpticL, a Python library that uses beam-path simulation and dynamic routing to enable adaptive, path-based layouts. They created modular optical baseplates for common subsystems and demonstrated a full laser system for strontium trapped ions.
result: The system achieved over 99% fidelity single-qubit gates and was used for laser cooling and qubit state detection, showing the feasibility of modular optical design.
conclusion: PyOpticL enables a new paradigm of design abstraction for optical systems, fostering open-source collaborative hardware design for AMO physics and quantum computing.

title: Strain-driven Transition From Correlated Insulating To Semimetallic States In Twisted-bilayer Graphene
authors: Lishuai Guo, Abulimiti Yasen, Mei Xiang, Wenliang Zhu And Minghu Pan
abstract: We investigate the interplay between Coulomb interaction and uniaxial heterostrain in twisted bilayer graphene (TBG) using a self-consistent Hartree–Fock (HF) approach projected onto the flat bands. For integer filling factors in the range of , we find that heterostrain strongly reconstructs the low-energy band structure and suppresses interaction-induced insulating gaps. As strain magnitude increases, the flat-band bandwidth is substantially enhanced, leading to an increased kinetic energy. The bandwidth enhancement effectively weakens the interaction strength relative to kinetic energy, resulting in the suppression of HF gaps and the emergence of semimetallic (SM) states. The strain effect can be primarily controlled by the filling factor, as well as the strain direction. At moderate strain strengths around 0.3% for , it can drive transitions between correlated insulating and SM states. In contrast, for , the HF gaps becomes negligible and the system remains essentially SM; both the strain direction and magnitude have negligible influence. Our results demonstrate that uniaxial heterostrain serves as an effective and versatile parameter for tuning correlated phases in TBG through the interplay of lattice deformation and Coulomb interactions.
tldr: This paper studies strain-driven transitions between correlated insulating and semimetallic states in twisted bilayer graphene using Hartree-Fock calculations.
motivation: Understanding how uniaxial heterostrain affects correlated phases in twisted bilayer graphene, which is a key material in condensed matter physics.
method: Self-consistent Hartree-Fock approach projected onto flat bands to compute band structure and interaction gaps under varying strain.
result: Strain enhances bandwidth and suppresses insulating gaps, driving transitions to semimetallic states; effect depends on filling factor and strain direction.
conclusion: Uniaxial heterostrain is an effective tuning parameter for correlated phases in twisted bilayer graphene.

title: Sorting Prolate And Oblate Spheroids With A Diatomic Gas In A Magnetic Field
authors: Ruben Lier
abstract: For a gas of diatomic particles with a nonzero magnetic moment, the Senftleben–Beenakker effect implies that transport can be affected by a magnetic field even when the particles are charge neutral. In such a gas, two independent anisotropic odd viscosities are allowed by symmetry and can have opposite signs. We study the resulting odd-viscous Stokes flow around spheroids in the regime where the odd viscosities are small compared to the shear viscosity. Using a perturbative expansion around the spherical solution and the Lorentz reciprocal theorem, we compute the lift forces on oblate and prolate spheroids for general values of the two odd viscosity coefficients. We show that the resulting Hall angles can differ for oblate and prolate spheroids, implying that sedimentation in a diatomic gas subject to a background magnetic field can separate particles according to shape.
tldr: This paper studies odd-viscous Stokes flow around spheroids in a diatomic gas under a magnetic field, showing shape-based separation via Hall angles.
motivation: Understanding how odd viscosities affect particle transport in neutral gases with magnetic moments, enabling shape-based separation.
method: Perturbative expansion around spherical solution and Lorentz reciprocal theorem to compute lift forces on spheroids for general odd viscosity coefficients.
result: Hall angles differ for oblate and prolate spheroids, allowing shape separation during sedimentation in a magnetic field.
conclusion: Odd viscosities in diatomic gases can be exploited to separate particles by shape, with potential applications in particle sorting.

title: Physical Sampling For Computational Photography
authors: Ni Chen And David J Brady
abstract: The standard model of photography is that lenses form images and focal planes capture those images. Over the past two decades, however, cameras have been transformed from devices that record focal images into analog-to-digital converters that transform massively parallel optical signals into serial electronic data. Under this new model, one may choose to maximize the quality and quantity of captured information, rather than focal image quality. Here we review the nature of the optical data stream and consider lens and focal plane designs that improve information capture capacity. After maximizing information capacity, the challenge of converting this information to digital data requires novel read-out and compression. We review strategies for approaching physical information limits under realistic size, power, and bandwidth constraints. Multiscale monocentric (spherical primary optics combined with arrays of secondary micro-cameras, each imaging a narrow subfield) and array lens architectures relax unfavorable geometric scaling by trading monolithic optics for co-designed system-level integration (jointly optimized optics, focal-plane, and readout subsystems). Metaoptic and mode-sorting focal plane filters implement richer projection operators that sample spectral, polarimetric, and coherence features without requiring exhaustive scanning. Finally, because readout and computation dominate energy at high throughput, we highlight architectures that perform dimensionality reduction before (or during) digitization, including integrated photonic encoders and multilayer optical projections coupled to detection and learned decoding. Together, these developments motivate a shift from cameras optimized to produce 2D images toward cameras engineered as end-to-end information channels, co-designing optics, focal-plane, and readout to deliver more task-relevant measurements per photon and per joule.
tldr: This paper reviews computational photography architectures that optimize information capture and compression under physical constraints, but does not address quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To improve camera design by maximizing information capacity and energy efficiency, moving beyond traditional focal imaging.
method: Reviews multiscale optics, metaoptic filters, and integrated photonic encoders that perform dimensionality reduction before digitization.
result: Proposes co-designed optics, focal-plane, and readout subsystems to deliver more task-relevant measurements per photon and per joule.
conclusion: Cameras should be engineered as end-to-end information channels rather than simple image recorders.

title: Green’s Function Methods For Computing Supercurrents In Josephson Junctions
authors: Eduardo R Mucciolo, Jouko Nieminen, Xiao Xiao, Wei-Chi Chiu, Michael N Leuenberger And Arun Bansil
abstract: Interest in Josephson junctions (JJs) has increased rapidly in recent years not only because of their use in qubits and other quantum devices but also due to the unique physics supported by the JJs. The advent of various novel quantum materials for both the barrier region and the superconducting leads has led to the possibility of adding new functionalities to the JJs. Thus, there is a growing need for accurate modeling of the JJs and related systems to enable their predictive control and atomistic level understanding. This review presents an in-depth discussion of a Green’s-function-based formalism for computing supercurrents in JJs. The formulation is tailored for large-scale atomistic simulations and encompasses both dc and ac supercurrents. We hope that this review will provide a timely and comprehensive reference for researchers as well as beginning practitioners interested in Green’s-function-based methods to model supercurrents in JJs.
tldr: A review of Green's function methods for computing supercurrents in Josephson junctions, focusing on large-scale atomistic simulations.
motivation: Josephson junctions are key components in qubits and quantum devices, and accurate modeling is needed for predictive control and atomistic understanding.
method: The paper presents a Green's-function-based formalism tailored for large-scale atomistic simulations to compute both dc and ac supercurrents.
result: The formalism enables accurate modeling of supercurrents in Josephson junctions with novel quantum materials.
conclusion: The review serves as a comprehensive reference for researchers and practitioners interested in Green's-function-based modeling of supercurrents.

title: Unlocking Complex Optical Vortices With Flat Optics
authors: Hammad Ahmed, Shumei Chen, Xibin Yang And Xianzhong Chen
abstract: Optical vortices (OVs) possess spiral wavefronts and quantized orbital angular momentum (OAM), allowing them to act as key carriers of information and enabling light to possess high-dimensional degrees of freedom. In the past decade, there has been a growing interest in investigating complex OVs. Nevertheless, conventional methods for generating such beams are limited by bulky setups, high costs, and restricted control. Optical metasurfaces have emerged as promising candidates to overcome these challenges in a compact and cost-effective platform with enhanced control. This review begins by presenting an advanced platform designed for manipulating OVs and then discusses emerging types of OVs, including composite, grafted, and comb-like structured light beams, as well as multispectral and arbitrarily shaped OVs, along with nonlinear metasurface approaches. Next, we review the recent progress in OAM detection and mode discrimination, highlighting current challenges for high-capacity OAM systems. After that, we emphasize key applications ranging from OAM-based holography for optical encryption to super-resolution microscopy, structured-light trapping, and quantum state engineering. Finally, we critically identify the key challenges and future prospects for metasurface-enabled OV technologies.
tldr: A review of metasurface-based generation and detection of complex optical vortices for high-dimensional information encoding.
motivation: Conventional methods for generating complex optical vortices are bulky and costly; metasurfaces offer a compact, cost-effective platform with enhanced control.
method: The paper reviews recent progress in metasurface designs for generating composite, grafted, comb-like, multispectral, and arbitrarily shaped optical vortices, as well as OAM detection and mode discrimination techniques.
result: Metasurface-enabled OV technologies enable applications in OAM-based holography, super-resolution microscopy, structured-light trapping, and quantum state engineering.
conclusion: Metasurfaces provide a promising platform for complex OV manipulation, but challenges remain in scalability, efficiency, and integration for high-capacity OAM systems.

title: Chiral Graviton Modes In Fermionic Fractional Chern Insulators
authors: Min Long, Zeno Bacciconi, Hongyu Lu, Hernan B Xavier, Zi Yang Meng And Marcello Dalmonte
abstract: Chiral graviton modes are hallmark collective excitations of fractional quantum Hall (FQH) liquids. However, their existence on the lattice, where continuum symmetries that protect them from decay are lost, is still an open and urgent question, especially considering the recent advances in the realization of fractional Chern insulators (FCI) in transition metal dichalcogenides and rhombohedral pentalayer graphene. Here we present a comprehensive theoretical and numerical study of graviton-modes in fermionic FCI, and thoroughly demonstrate their existence. We first derive a lattice stress tensor operator in the context of the fermionic Harper–Hofstadter (HH) model which captures the graviton in the flat band limit. Importantly, we discover that such lattice stress-tensor operators are deeply connected to correlation hole dynamics, readily generalizable to generic Chern bands. We then explicitly show the adiabatic connection between FQH and FCI chiral graviton modes by interpolating from a low flux HH model to a Checkerboard lattice model that hosts a topological flat band. In particular, using state-of-the-art matrix product state and exact diagonalization simulations, we provide strong evidence that chiral graviton modes are long-lived excitations in FCIs despite the lack of continuous symmetries and the scattering with a two-magnetoroton continuum. By means of a careful finite-size analysis, we show that the lattice generates an intrinsic decay rate for the graviton mode which is small compared to its energy. We discuss the relevance of our results for the exploration of graviton modes in FCI phases realized in solid state settings, experimental utility on diagnosis of fractional topological phases, as well as cold atom experiments.
tldr: This paper studies chiral graviton modes in fractional Chern insulators, a topic in condensed matter physics with no direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To determine whether chiral graviton modes, hallmark excitations of fractional quantum Hall liquids, exist in lattice fractional Chern insulators despite the lack of continuous symmetries.
method: Derives a lattice stress tensor operator for the Harper-Hofstadter model, uses matrix product state and exact diagonalization simulations to study the adiabatic connection between FQH and FCI graviton modes.
result: Provides strong evidence that chiral graviton modes are long-lived excitations in FCIs, with a small intrinsic decay rate compared to their energy.
conclusion: The results are relevant for exploring graviton modes in FCI phases in solid-state and cold atom experiments, but do not advance quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Vortex Solitons In Disclination Quasicrystals
authors: Hua Zhong, Yaroslav V Kartashov, Yongdong Li, Fangwei Ye And Yiqi Zhang
abstract: Quasicrystals are ubiquitous in nature. They represent unique aperiodic materials featuring long-range order that occupy an intermediate niche between exactly periodic and disordered materials. These properties are reflected in the unusual evolutionary dynamics of excitations and unique localization properties of linear eigenmodes supported by quasicrystals. In particular, being the structures characterized by discrete rotational symmetry of order , photonic quasicrystals can support the stable propagation of linear vortex-carrying light beams and vortex solitons. However, the impact of discrete rotational symmetry of quasicrystals on the properties of vortex light states has not been investigated so far, as only the systems constructed using the simplest Penrose tiling or corresponding optically induced Penrose lattices are considered in this context. Here, we propose a broad class of quasicrystals with global topological defects—disclinations—introduced into their structure that allows to produce novel quasicrystalline structures with any desired order of discrete rotational symmetry from the basic Penrose structure. Such global topological deformation substantially enriches the linear spectrum of quasicrystals, allowing them to support new types of linear vortex states and bifurcating from them families of stable thresholdless vortex solitons with unusual intensity and phase distributions. We find two different classes of stable vortex solitons comprising in-phase or out-of-phase pairs of closely located bright spots, with total intensity distribution reflecting a particular discrete rotational symmetry of the quasicrystal with disclination. Remarkably, even low-charge vortex solitons can be stable in quasicrystals with disclinations, whereas stability intervals for them broaden with the decrease of the discrete rotational symmetry of quasicrystals. Our results extend the theory of localization in quasicrystals to structures with global topological deformation, highlighting emerging prospects for the robust transmission of power or information arising in these systems.
tldr: This paper studies vortex solitons in photonic quasicrystals with disclinations, focusing on their stability and intensity distributions.
motivation: To understand how global topological defects (disclinations) in quasicrystals affect the properties of vortex light states, which have not been investigated before.
method: The authors propose a class of quasicrystals with disclinations, analyze their linear spectrum, and numerically find families of stable vortex solitons.
result: Two classes of stable vortex solitons are found, with stability intervals broadening as discrete rotational symmetry decreases.
conclusion: The results extend localization theory to quasicrystals with topological deformations, suggesting potential for robust transmission of power or information.

title: Gravitational And Other Shifts Of Whispering-gallery And Gravitational State Interference Patterns Of Light Neutral Particles
authors: V V Nesvizhevsky, J A Pioquinto, K Schreiner, S Baeßler, P Crivelli, F Nez, S Reynaud, P Yzombard, S A Vasiliev And E Widmann
abstract: We discuss the interference patterns of gravitational and whispering gallery quantum states that can be observed with neutrons, atoms, antiatoms, muonium (Mu), positronium (Ps), and other light neutral particles. A gravitational shift of interference patterns of neutron gravitational and whispering-gallery states can be easily observed with cold, very cold, or ultracold neutrons. The developed methods can be used for observing/searching for other shifts in fundamental neutron physics experiments, for instance, for measuring the gravitational constant or constraining the neutron electric charge. A series of such measurements will be made with neutrons at the PF1B, PF2, D17 facilities at the ILL. A peculiar feature of analogous atomic (anti-atomic) experiments is the much smaller effective critical energies of the materials of mirrors for (anti)atoms. We evaluated parameters that make a measurement of the hydrogen and antihydrogen whispering-gallery states and their gravitational shifts feasible. A series of such measurements will be made with hydrogen and deuterium atoms by the GRASIAN collaboration in Vienna and Turku. A similar measurement with antihydrogen atoms may be of interest for the GBAR experiment, the ASACUSA experiment, which is producing a beam of slow antihydrogen atoms, and other experiments at CERN that study the gravitational properties of antimatter. Quantum reflection (QR) of Mu and Ps from material surfaces opens the possibility of observing whispering-gallery states, although such measurements remain experimentally challenging. Because of the small masses of Mu and Ps, their effective critical energies of the mirror materials are much higher for them than the effective critical energies for hydrogen and other atoms. The observation of gravitational shifts of such states is particularly demanding because of the extremely short lifetimes of these systems. Measurements of whispering gallery states with all these atoms and particles yield precise and detailed information on the QR properties of materials, providing valuable input for both fundamental physics and surface physics studies.
tldr: This paper discusses gravitational and whispering gallery state interference patterns for light neutral particles, focusing on experimental measurements with neutrons, atoms, and antiatoms.
motivation: To explore gravitational shifts and other effects in quantum states of neutral particles, which could provide tests of fundamental physics and surface properties.
method: The authors analyze interference patterns of gravitational and whispering gallery states using quantum reflection and evaluate experimental feasibility for various particles.
result: They find that gravitational shifts can be observed with neutrons and that measurements with hydrogen and antihydrogen are feasible, while muonium and positronium remain challenging due to short lifetimes.
conclusion: These measurements can yield precise information on quantum reflection and fundamental constants, but the work is primarily experimental and phenomenological without deep information-theoretic or thermodynamic contributions.

title: Inferring The Underlying Higher-order Network Structure From Low-resolution Interaction State Data
authors: Chuang Ma, Xiao-Feng Luo, Rui-Hui He, Dao-Yu Li, Hai-Feng Zhang And Gui-Quan Sun
abstract: Network reconstruction aims to infer the underlying interactions between entities from observed data and serves as a cornerstone of network science. While most existing methods focus on dynamics-based data and primarily target binary interactions, real-world data often reflect coarse-grained interaction states of individuals over specific time intervals and may involve complex multi-body interactions beyond pairwise connections. Reconstructing the underlying higher-order network structure from such low-resolution interaction state data is therefore of critical importance. In this paper, we formulate an optimization model for inferring higher-order structures based on the minimum description length principle. To solve this problem, we propose a Bayesian network reconstruction method that integrates distribution estimation with Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling. Our method begins by generating candidate configurations for each time interval via MCMC sampling, then constructs a Bayesian network—guided by minimum-entropy—to capture dependencies between configurations across different time intervals. Finally, an iterative update strategy based on distribution estimation is employed to approach the optimal solution. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method.
tldr: This paper proposes a Bayesian method to infer higher-order network structures from low-resolution interaction state data using minimum description length and MCMC sampling.
motivation: Existing network reconstruction methods focus on binary interactions and dynamics-based data, but real-world data often involve coarse-grained interaction states and multi-body interactions.
method: The method uses MCMC sampling to generate candidate configurations per time interval, builds a Bayesian network guided by minimum-entropy to capture dependencies, and iteratively updates via distribution estimation.
result: Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the method's effectiveness and robustness in reconstructing higher-order network structures.
conclusion: The proposed approach successfully infers higher-order interactions from low-resolution data, addressing a gap in network reconstruction.

title: Rashba-like Spin Splitting In Inversion Symmetric Plasmonic Metasurface
authors: Sujit Rajak, Nishkarsh Kumar, Dheeraj Yadav, Suman Mandal, Jeeban K Nayak, Ayan Banerjee, Subhasish Dutta Gupta, Olivier Martin And Nirmalya Ghosh
abstract: Spin-dependent dispersion and Rashba effect are manifestations of spin–orbit interaction (SOI) associated with the breaking of the spatial inversion symmetry in condensed matter and in optical systems. Here, we report an extraordinary spin-split dispersion effect of leaky surface plasmons in an inversion-symmetric plasmonic crystal. Momentum domain polarization analysis identified a transverse momentum-dependent linear birefringence–linear dichroism (geometric LB–LD) effect responsible for this phenomena. It is demonstrated that evolution of strong geometrical phase gradient due to the geometric LB–LD effect mediates the spin-split dispersion in inversion symmetric plasmonic metasurface through spin (circular polarization)-dependent transverse momentum. This unconventional SOI phenomena offers a new paradigm of spin-based dispersion engineering and spin-controlled nano-optical functionalities by encompassing the forbidden class of symmetric metastructures in the realm of spin optics.
tldr: This paper reports a spin-split dispersion effect in an inversion-symmetric plasmonic metasurface due to geometric phase gradients, demonstrating a new spin-orbit interaction phenomenon.
motivation: To explore spin-dependent dispersion and Rashba-like effects in optical systems without spatial inversion symmetry breaking, enabling new spin-controlled nano-optical functionalities.
method: Momentum domain polarization analysis is used to identify a transverse momentum-dependent linear birefringence–linear dichroism (geometric LB–LD) effect, and the evolution of geometrical phase gradient is studied.
result: A strong geometrical phase gradient due to the geometric LB–LD effect mediates spin-split dispersion in an inversion-symmetric plasmonic metasurface through spin-dependent transverse momentum.
conclusion: This unconventional spin-orbit interaction offers a new paradigm for spin-based dispersion engineering and spin-controlled nano-optical functionalities using symmetric metastructures.

title: Machine-learning-enabled Solvent Engineering For Uniform Quantum Dot Packing In Efficient And Stable Quantum-dot Light-emitting Diodes
authors: Beomsoo Chun, Byong Jae Kim, Hyeongjin Kim, Jeong Han Song, Yeongsik Kim, Jaehoon Lim And Jeonghun Kwak
abstract: Colloidal quantum dots (QDs) offer size-tunable optoelectronic properties and solution processability, yet achieving uniformly packed emissive layers remains a bottleneck for high-performance quantum-dot light-emitting diodes (QLEDs). Here, we report a machine learning -guided solvent optimization strategy to produce homogeneous QD films. Five representative solvent parameters are evaluated, and multiple regression models are trained against film uniformity derived from atomic force microscopy. Among them, support vector regression provides the highest predictive accuracy for film homogeneity. Guided by these predictions, we formulate a mixed solvent that closely matches the target profile, yielding superior packing homogeneity, which is confirmed by grazing-incidence small-angle x-ray scattering. QLEDs fabricated with this formulation exhibit an external quantum efficiency of 20.6% and an operational lifetime of 468.5 h at 20 000 cd m−2, surpassing all single-solvent controls. These findings establish packing homogeneity as a decisive factor for device performance and introduce a generalizable and scalable framework for data-driven design of solution-processed devices, holding strong potential for next-generation optoelectronic systems.
tldr: This paper uses machine learning to optimize solvent mixtures for uniform quantum dot packing in QLEDs, achieving high efficiency and stability.
motivation: Achieving uniformly packed emissive layers is a bottleneck for high-performance quantum-dot light-emitting diodes (QLEDs).
method: Five solvent parameters were evaluated, and multiple regression models (including support vector regression) were trained to predict film uniformity from atomic force microscopy data; a mixed solvent was formulated based on predictions.
result: QLEDs fabricated with the optimized solvent exhibited an external quantum efficiency of 20.6% and an operational lifetime of 468.5 h at 20,000 cd m−2, outperforming single-solvent controls.
conclusion: Packing homogeneity is a decisive factor for device performance, and the data-driven framework is generalizable for solution-processed devices.

title: Uniaxial-stress-induced Magnetic Transitions In The Triangular-lattice Antiferromagnet PdCrO2
authors: Nina Stilkerich, Tobias Ritschel, Hilary M L Noad, Richard Waite, Dmitry Khalyavin, Kousuke Ishida, Pascal Manuel, Fabio Orlandi, Seunghyun Khim, Elena Gati, Andrew P Mackenzie, Jochen Geck And Clifford W Hicks
abstract: Uniaxial stress is a promising method to tune magnetic frustration, allowing its effects to be studied in a precise way. In this work, uniaxial stress is applied to the triangular-lattice antiferromagnet PdCrO . The Cr–Cr magnetic interaction is very sensitive to interatomic separation, so laboratory-achievable stress can induce substantial changes in magnetic structure. Results from three types of measurement are presented: x-ray diffraction, the stress–strain relationship, and neutron diffraction. The combined data show that the elastic moduli of PdCrO are strongly affected by stress-induced changes in magnetic structure. A new, first-order stress-induced magnetic transition is observed, at which the lattice constant shrinks by 0.21%. The lattice stiffens dramatically across this transition: the Young’s modulus increases by GPa, and the Poisson ratio falls from to . This stiffening indicates that the magnetic order ‘locks,’ that is, becomes insensitive to lattice strain. This locking might occur because the new stress-induced magnetic order nests the Fermi surface of the Pd sheets. Other frustrated magnets, including candidate spin liquids, may show similarly strong coupling between magnetic and elastic degrees of freedom.
tldr: This paper studies stress-induced magnetic transitions in the triangular-lattice antiferromagnet PdCrO2, focusing on magnetoelastic coupling.
motivation: To understand how uniaxial stress can tune magnetic frustration and induce new magnetic orders in frustrated magnets.
method: Combined x-ray diffraction, stress-strain measurements, and neutron diffraction under uniaxial stress.
result: A first-order stress-induced magnetic transition is observed, accompanied by a 0.21% lattice shrinkage and dramatic stiffening of the lattice.
conclusion: The magnetic order becomes locked under stress, possibly due to Fermi surface nesting, suggesting strong magnetoelastic coupling in frustrated magnets.

title: Polarity And Fabrication Effects In Ar‐bombarded GaN
authors: Przemysław Jóźwik, Katharina Lorenz, Ewa Grzanka, Afonso Caçador, Joanna Matulewicz, Mikołaj Grabowski, Cyprian Mieszczyński, Renata Ratajczak, Andrzej Turos And Mike Leszczynski
abstract: This study investigates the response of various types of gallium nitride (GaN) crystals to ion irradiation, a process that is pertinent to the reliability of materials utilised in high-power electronic devices. Two types of c-oriented GaN, which were grown by ammonothermal method and hydride vapour phase epitaxy, were irradiated with 300 kV Ar ions. The influence of crystal polarity on the resulting damage was evaluated using ion channelling measurements supported by Monte Carlo simulations. The experimental data demonstrate significant disparities in the accumulation of disorder between the two materials. Ammonothermal GaN, despite its lower initial threading dislocation density, exhibits a faster increase in lattice disorder, consistent with the formation of point defects and small defect clusters. Hydride-grown GaN exhibits a distinct behaviour, with the channelling signal denoting the presence of extended defects, such as dislocation loops, that persist up to a fluence of 3 × 1015 cm−2. Signatures of point-defect-dominated disorder emerge only at even higher fluences. In the case of ammonothermal material, the polarity-related differences in disorder remain minor and are largely within the experimental uncertainties. By contrast, for hydride-grown GaN, the N-polar samples consistently exhibit higher damage levels than their Ga-polar counterparts. The significant increase in disorder observed at the highest fluence points to the initiation of plastic deformation, suggesting conditions that are conducive to substantial structural modifications.
tldr: This paper studies ion irradiation damage in GaN crystals, focusing on polarity and fabrication effects.
motivation: Understanding radiation damage in GaN is important for reliability of high-power electronic devices.
method: GaN samples grown by ammonothermal and HVPE methods were irradiated with Ar ions; damage was characterized by ion channelling and Monte Carlo simulations.
result: Ammonothermal GaN shows faster disorder accumulation via point defects, while HVPE GaN exhibits extended defects; polarity effects are minor in ammonothermal but significant in HVPE GaN.
conclusion: The study reveals material-dependent damage mechanisms and polarity effects, relevant for device design.

title: Phase-controlled Direct Laser Acceleration Enabled By Longitudinal Variation Of The Laser-driven Quasi-static Plasma Magnetic Field
authors: R Bhakta, I-L Yeh, K Tangtartharakul, L Willingale And A Arefiev
abstract: Direct laser acceleration (DLA) enables energy transfer from an ultra-high-intensity laser to plasma electrons and underpins many laser-driven particle and radiation-source concepts. A laser-driven azimuthal plasma magnetic field is a key player in this process: it confines energetic electrons, induces betatron oscillations, and makes possible a resonant interaction between the betatron motion and the laser field. While this betatron resonance can enhance electron energy gain, the gain itself generally drives frequency detuning and promotes largely reversible energy exchange that limits net acceleration. Here we show, using a test-electron model with prescribed fields, that a slow longitudinal increase of the quasi-static plasma magnetic field qualitatively changes DLA by introducing hysteresis in the ratio of the betatron frequency to the laser frequency experienced by the electron, so that this ratio depends on the prior evolution of the electron even at the same energy. This hysteresis enables phase control of the electron-laser energy exchange and suppresses the usual reversibility of DLA, allowing electrons to retain the acquired energy and sustain energy gain without intermittent losses.
tldr: This paper studies phase-controlled direct laser acceleration using longitudinal variation of a plasma magnetic field, a topic in plasma physics and laser-driven particle acceleration.
motivation: Direct laser acceleration (DLA) is important for laser-driven particle and radiation sources, but energy gain is limited by reversible energy exchange. The authors aim to overcome this limitation.
method: Using a test-electron model with prescribed fields, they simulate the effect of a slowly increasing quasi-static plasma magnetic field on electron dynamics.
result: The longitudinal increase introduces hysteresis in the betatron-to-laser frequency ratio, enabling phase control and suppressing reversibility, allowing sustained energy gain.
conclusion: This approach could improve the efficiency of laser-driven accelerators and radiation sources.
